implementation_notes: Spring supplies the dispatcher: application code publishes any POJO (no ApplicationEvent subclass needed) through ApplicationEventPublisher, listeners are @EventListener methods resolved by parameter type, and @TransactionalEventListener binds a listener to BEFORE_COMMIT / AFTER_COMMIT / AFTER_ROLLBACK so the reaction can run once the state is committed. Spring Data adds the aggregate-side half: @DomainEvents marks the method exposing collected events and the repository publishes them on save(). The classic registry disappears; what remains to decide is the publication phase and listener ordering.
pitfalls: A plain @EventListener runs synchronously in the publisher's transaction, so an exception in the listener rolls back the aggregate change - usually not what the listener's author expects.
An event published outside an active transaction is discarded by @TransactionalEventListener unless fallbackExecution = true is set.

variants.name: Sealed interface + records + exhaustive switch dispatch (framework-free)
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface OrderEvent permits ... + record events + exhaustive switch
variants.implementation_notes: Framework-free Java: model the closed event set as a sealed interface with record implementations and dispatch with a switch over the sealed type, which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness under Java 21 pattern matching (on Java 17 the same hierarchy works with a visitor or an instanceof chain). Reactions with side effects stay in a small dispatcher class or handler map, and publication timing is whatever the unit of work does. Choose it for libraries and for applications that keep Spring out of the domain layer.
pitfalls: Sealed hierarchies are closed by design: another module or plugin cannot add an event type, so an externally extensible event set needs an open interface plus a documented unknown-type policy.
Records are shallow-immutable: a record whose component is a List<T> lets handlers mutate the event's members.
